strengths: Novel geometric insight: elegant product structure decomposition of the Cholesky manifold opens a principled design space for new metrics
Complete mathematical framework with closed-form expressions for all Riemannian operators and rigorous proofs
Significant numerical stability advantage: remains stable down to ε=10^-30 where LCM completely fails
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (SPDNet, GyroSPD, RResNet) with proper ablations and scalability analysis
Honest reporting with dataset-dependent sensitivity analysis connecting deformation parameter θ to Cholesky diagonal statistics
Clear presentation with excellent organization and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Modest practical improvements with inconsistent gains across datasets (2-3.5% on benchmarks); benefits often within typical variance
Straightforward application of product metric framework: proposed metrics are natural but not creative instantiations of the design principle
Requires dataset-specific θ tuning without principled selection guidance, adding hyperparameter complexity that undermines practical utility
Experimental design concerns: differential preprocessing (matrix power -0.25 applied selectively) and post-hoc design choices reduce transparency of comparisons
Limited application scope: small datasets (≤93×93 matrices, ≤45 classes), simple network components, no evaluation on modern large-scale SPD learning tasks
Theoretical limitations underexplored: locally-defined geodesics and restrictive assumptions on gyro operations (Lem. 3.6) lack systematic analysis of when violations occur
Numerical stability results use extreme ε values (10^-30) far beyond typical precision issues; practical relevance for well-conditioned real matrices unclear
Unclear guidance on metric selection: when should practitioners use BWCM over PCM given marginal differences in Table 14?
Code unavailable at review time and some hyperparameter choices appear ad-hoc (e.g., weight decay selectively applied)

strengths: Clear mathematical framework: Product structure of Cholesky manifold is well-characterized and enables principled metric design with complete closed-form Riemannian operators
Demonstrable numerical stability: Table 5 shows compelling robustness improvements—remaining stable to ε=1e^-30 vs LCM failure at ε=1e^-3—with quantifiable metrics
Comprehensive and reproducible: Complete mathematical derivations, proofs in appendices, detailed experimental settings, promised code release, thorough ablation studies
Solid experimental validation: Consistent positive improvements across multiple datasets (Radar, HDM05, FPHA) and architectures (SPDNet, GyroSPD, RResNet) with proper statistical reporting
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Product structure insight, while clean, is a straightforward application of product metric theory to the block structure of Cholesky factors. Metrics proposed are direct pullbacks of existing metrics to individual R++ factors. Using diagonal powers instead of logs/exponentials is a practical algorithmic trick rather than a fundamental conceptual contribution

Unclear practical significance of main claimed advantage: Extreme numerical stability tests (ε=1e^-15 to 1e^-30) are unrealistic for typical ML applications. Paper does not demonstrate that the tested datasets actually require this extreme stability, nor clearly show that practical improvements stem from stability rather than simply using more numerically efficient operations

Modest empirical improvements with unclear patterns: Accuracy gains over LCM range from 0.75% to 3.6% with high dataset dependence. Improvements are negligible on some tasks (FPHA on GyroSPD). Standard deviations sometimes overlap with baselines. No clear pattern explaining when methods should be preferred

Incomplete experimental analysis: (1) BWCM consistently underperforms PCM without explanation; (2) Optimal θ varies wildly across datasets (-2 to +1.5, Table 7), indicating significant hyperparameter sensitivity that undermines the 'closed-form advantage' claim; (3) Limited task diversity (only action recognition and radar); (4) No evaluation on applications mentioned in introduction (medical imaging, brain connectivity, EEG)

Significant theoretical gaps: No convergence analysis, no principled method for θ selection (requires per-dataset empirical tuning), gyrovector axioms require positivity constraints needing 'numeric tricks' (Remark 3.9) that defeat elegance of closed-form operators. Theorems 3.2-3.3 are mechanical applications of product metric theory rather than novel insights

Presentation and clarity issues: Dense notation (60+ symbols) hinders accessibility; Figure 1 is ineffective; key mechanisms (why powers improve stability?) unexplained; unclear practical guidance on metric selection; missing mechanistic explanation for dataset-dependent improvements from diagonal statistics analysis

strengths: Elegant discovery of product structure on Cholesky manifold that opens principled design space for new metrics via choice on R++
Comprehensive mathematical development with all Riemannian operators (geodesics, exp/log maps, parallel transport, Fréchet means) derived in closed form
Compelling numerical stability advantages: proposed metrics stable to ε=1e-30 for small matrices vs ε=1e-3 for diagonal log metric (Table 5)
Thorough experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (Radar, HDM05, FPHA) and architectures (SPDNet, GyroSPD, RResNet) with systematic ablations
Insightful analysis connecting dataset-dependent θ preference to Cholesky diagonal statistics (Section E.4)
Scalability analysis showing clear computational advantages at high dimensions (Tables 12-13), making metrics practical for large-scale problems
Strong reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameter tables, and clear experimental methodology (5-fold CV with error bars)
Metrics integrate seamlessly into existing frameworks (MLR classifiers, residual blocks) without architectural changes
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of final metrics: θ-PCM and M-DBWM are relatively straightforward applications of power metrics and GBWM to Cholesky diagonal once product structure identified
Empirical improvements are modest on several benchmarks (Radar SPDNet: 95.79% vs 93.49% for LCM) and dataset-dependent without principled selection method
Lack of principled guidance for parameter selection: requires dataset-specific tuning of θ (Table 7) without theoretical framework for a priori choice
No principled justification for why power-based deformations should outperform other choices beyond empirical observation
Gyrovector structures have practical limitations requiring constraints on L, K and 'numeric tricks' (clamping) to ensure well-definedness (Remark 3.9), undermining theoretical elegance
Incomplete comparison with recent work: adaptive log-Euclidean (Chen et al. 2024d) and GBWM mentioned but not empirically compared
Tensor interpolation experiment (E.2) feels supplementary: visual interpretation of Figure 2 is unclear and practical significance for main applications not established
Geodesics are only locally defined {t ∈ R|L + tθX ∈ D^n_++} with no discussion of implications for optimization algorithms and step size selection
θ-BWCM sometimes underperforms θ-PCM (e.g., Tables 2-3) with no clear guidance on metric selection
Dense presentation with many theorems and heavy notation (M-DBW, (θ,M)-DBWM) makes roadmap from product structure insight to practical metrics harder to follow
